full_title: PEOPLE OF THE PHILIPPINES, PLAINTIFF-APPELLEE, VS. RONALD N. RICKETTS, CYRUS PAUL S. VALENZUELA, MANUEL J. MANGUBAT, JOSEPH D. ARNALDO, AND GLENN S. PEREZ, ACCUSED, RONALD N. RICKETTS AND GLENN S. PEREZ, ACCUSED-APPELLANTS.
subject: Criminal Law
syllabus_topic: IV. Special Penal Laws > E. Anti-Graft and Corrupt Practices Act (RA 3019, as amended by BP 195 and RA 10910)
topics: Conspiracy must be proved beyond reasonable doubt
No presumption of bad faith in R.A. 3019 cases; accused's silence does not shift the burden
Release of seized items held in custodia legis under the OMB Act (R.A. 9239)

other_subjects.subject: Remedial Law, Legal and Judicial Ethics
other_subjects.syllabus_topic: VIII. Evidence > E. Kinds (Rule 130) > 3. Testimonial Evidence > f. Hearsay Rule; Exceptions

doctrine:
**Under the doctrine of independently relevant statements, a witness's testimony that a third person told him something is admissible only to prove that the statement was made, not that it is true;** as to the truth of what was said, it remains hearsay. A security guard's report that the accused employee, caught removing seized items, said that the "Chairman" ordered the removal proves the employee's unauthorized act and that he made the statement. It does not prove that the Chairman gave the order (reiterated, citing XXX v. People and Gubaton v. Amador).

**Conspiracy must be proved beyond reasonable doubt**, through overt acts showing a conscious common design; mere knowledge, acquiescence, or agreement to cooperate is not enough (Macairan v. People, reiterated). There is **no presumption of bad faith** in prosecutions under R.A. No. 3019. The accused's failure to testify does not shift the burden of proof, and a public officer enjoys the presumption of innocence like any other accused.

A public officer who, without written authority, takes out and returns to the owner items seized and held in preventive custody (custodia legis) under Section 10(e) of R.A. No. 9239 acts with manifest partiality and evident bad faith and **gives the owner unwarranted benefits under Section 3(e) of R.A. No. 3019**. It is immaterial that some items remained in custody or that the seizure might later be questioned; whether the items were pirated or admissible is for the OMB and the courts to decide.
facts:
Ronald Ricketts was Chairman and CEO of the Optical Media Board (OMB); Glenn Perez was an OMB Computer Operator. On May 27, 2010, OMB agents, Perez among them, raided a compound in Quiapo, Manila on a report that pirated optical discs were stored there. They seized 127 boxes and two sacks of DVDs and VCDs, a recording machine, and an Isuzu Elf van marked "Sky High Marketing." The seized items were brought to the OMB compound, turned over to the guard on duty, and recorded in the logbook.

At about 10:00 p.m. that day, guard Pedro Gazzingan found Perez reloading 121 boxes of the seized items onto the van. Asked for the gate pass required by OMB standard procedure, Perez had none and said that it was "Chairman" (Ricketts) who had told him to take the items out. Executive Director Valenzuela, the ranking officer on duty, reportedly told the guard, "kung utos ni Chairman, wala tayong magagawa." The next day only four boxes remained.

Ricketts, Perez, Valenzuela and two other OMB officers were charged with violating Section 3(e) of R.A. No. 3019 for giving Sky High Marketing unwarranted benefits by releasing the seized discs. Valenzuela's demurrer to evidence was granted. Ricketts and Perez did not testify. Because the Sandiganbayan division could not reach a unanimous decision, a special division of five justices was formed. On March 15, 2019, it acquitted the two other officers but convicted Ricketts and Perez, sentencing each to imprisonment of six years and one day to eight years, with perpetual disqualification from public office.

On appeal, Ricketts argued that the guard's account of what Perez said was hearsay and that conspiracy was not proved. He also questioned the procedure of the special division. Perez argued that the government suffered no prejudice because the warrantless seizure made the discs inadmissible anyway, it was not certain that the discs were pirated, their ownership was not established, and some discs remained in OMB custody.
issues: Whether the prosecution proved beyond reasonable doubt that Ricketts conspired with Perez, when the only evidence of his participation was the guard's account of what Perez told him.
Whether the prosecution proved beyond reasonable doubt all the elements of Section 3(e) of R.A. No. 3019 against Perez.
ruling:
**1. No; Ricketts must be acquitted.** The prosecution's theory of conspiracy rested solely on Gazzingan's report that Perez said Chairman Ricketts had ordered the pull-out, together with Ricketts' failure to deny it specifically at trial. Although Ricketts did not testify, he kept the presumption of innocence, and the prosecution kept the burden of proof: "there is no such thing as presumption of bad faith in cases involving violations of RA No. 3019." The report is an independently relevant statement only as to the fact that Perez made the statement. Gazzingan had no personal knowledge of who ordered the pull-out, so as to the truth of the statement the report is hearsay. **It proves Perez's unauthorized act but not that Ricketts ordered it, nor that a conspiracy existed.** Conspiracy requires proof beyond reasonable doubt of overt acts showing a conscious common design (Macairan v. People). The only overt acts proved were Perez's pull-out and the guard's act of allowing it, even though the guard had the power to stop a pull-out made without a gate pass. Ricketts' participation was "purely speculative and hearsay," and convicting him was a grievous error. Since Ricketts was acquitted, the Court found it unnecessary to discuss his procedural objections.

**2. Yes; Perez's conviction stands.** The elements of Section 3(e) are: (1) the accused is a public officer discharging administrative, judicial or official functions; (2) he acted with manifest partiality, evident bad faith, or gross inexcusable negligence; and (3) his action caused undue injury to any party, including the government, or gave a private party unwarranted benefits, advantage or preference. Perez was a public officer and part of the raiding team, so he knew that the discs were in OMB's preventive custody under Section 10(e) of R.A. No. 9239. Such items may be returned only after 30 days unless a case is filed (Section 3, Rule 7 of the IRR) and must be destroyed if found to violate the law (Section 23). Yet he took them out after office hours without written authority and returned them. This was manifest partiality and evident bad faith, and it gave Sky High Marketing unwarranted benefits before the OMB could review the discs and file the proper case. **It is immaterial that he did not take all the discs; what matters is that he interfered with property in custodia legis before legal processes could run**, depriving the government of the right to have the discs destroyed if the owners were found liable. Whether the discs were pirated, whether Sky High violated R.A. No. 9239, and whether the discs would be admissible were matters for the OMB and the courts, not Perez, to decide. His arguments on these points amounted to admitting that he released the discs without authority.
disposition: Ricketts' appeal was GRANTED, and the Sandiganbayan Decision dated March 15, 2019 and Resolution dated November 15, 2019 in Case No. SB-15-CRM-0132 were AFFIRMED with MODIFICATION. Ricketts was ACQUITTED for failure of the prosecution to prove conspiracy and his guilt beyond reasonable doubt; the hold departure order against him was lifted and his cash bond released, and entry of judgment as to him was ordered issued immediately. Perez's conviction for violation of Section 3(e) of R.A. No. 3019, with imprisonment of six years and one day as minimum to eight years as maximum and perpetual disqualification from holding public office, was AFFIRMED in toto.

bar_questions.q: Director Lim heads a government regulatory office. One night, security guard Tomas caught Officer Reyes loading confiscated goods into a private truck without the required gate pass. When challenged, Reyes told Tomas, "Director Lim ordered me to release these." Tomas let the truck go and wrote a report. Lim and Reyes were charged as conspirators with violating Section 3(e) of R.A. No. 3019. At trial, Tomas testified on what Reyes told him. No other evidence linked Lim to the release, and Lim did not testify. (a) Is Tomas's testimony on Reyes's statement admissible against Lim? (b) May Lim be convicted?

alac.answer: (a) It is admissible only to prove that Reyes made the statement, not that Lim actually gave the order; on that point it is hearsay. (b) No. Lim must be acquitted because conspiracy was not proved beyond reasonable doubt.
alac.legal_basis: Under the doctrine of independently relevant statements, only the fact that a statement was made is relevant; its truth or falsity is immaterial. Such a statement is admissible to prove that it was made, but it is hearsay as to the truth of what it asserts when the witness has no personal knowledge of it. Conspiracy must be proved by the same quantum as the crime, beyond reasonable doubt, through overt acts showing a conscious common design. (People v. Ricketts, G.R. No. 250867, March 16, 2022, citing XXX v. People and Macairan v. People)
alac.application: Tomas personally saw Reyes loading the goods and personally heard Reyes say that Lim ordered it, so he may testify to those facts. He has no personal knowledge of whether Lim actually gave any order, so on that point his testimony is hearsay. With no other evidence of an overt act by Lim, his participation is speculative. Lim's silence at trial does not supply the missing proof. He keeps the presumption of innocence, and there is no presumption of bad faith under R.A. No. 3019.
alac.conclusion: Tomas's testimony proves only that Reyes made the statement, and Lim must be acquitted.

bar_questions.q: Agent Bautista of the Optical Media Board took part in a raid that seized 100 boxes of suspected pirated DVDs, which were placed in OMB preventive custody. That night, without any written authority, he loaded 90 boxes back into the owner's van and let the owner drive away. Charged under Section 3(e) of R.A. No. 3019, Bautista argues that (1) the government suffered no prejudice because ten boxes remained, which were enough to support a case; and (2) the raid was conducted without a search warrant, so the discs would have been inadmissible anyway, and no one has proved that they were pirated. Are his defenses tenable?

alac.answer: No. His defenses do not negate the elements of Section 3(e) of R.A. No. 3019.
alac.legal_basis: Section 3(e) of R.A. No. 3019 punishes a public officer who, through manifest partiality, evident bad faith or gross inexcusable negligence, causes undue injury to any party, including the government, or gives a private party unwarranted benefits. Optical media taken into preventive custody under Section 10(e) of R.A. No. 9239 are in custodia legis and may be returned only as the law and its implementing rules allow. If they are found to violate the law, they are to be destroyed (Section 23). In People v. Ricketts (G.R. No. 250867, March 16, 2022), the Court held that an OMB employee who took out and returned seized discs without written authority acted with manifest partiality and evident bad faith and gave unwarranted benefits. It was immaterial that he did not take all the discs, and whether the discs were pirated or admissible was for the OMB and the courts, not the accused, to decide.
alac.application: Bautista knew the discs were in OMB custody because he took part in the seizure. Releasing 90 boxes at night without written authority favored the owner and shows a dishonest purpose, which is evident bad faith. The release gave the owner an unwarranted benefit and interfered with the OMB's processes before any case could be filed, depriving the government of the remedy of destruction. That ten boxes remained does not cure the interference. His arguments on the warrantless raid and the nature of the discs are questions for the OMB and the courts; raising them only confirms that he released the discs without authority.
alac.conclusion: Bautista's defenses fail, and he may be convicted of violating Section 3(e) of R.A. No. 3019.

bar_questions.q: Mayor Cruz and his driver were charged as conspirators under Section 3(e) of R.A. No. 3019 for the release of impounded logs from the municipal compound. The only evidence linking the mayor was a guard's testimony that the driver, caught hauling the logs, said the mayor had authorized it. The trial court convicted the mayor, reasoning that (1) he chose not to take the witness stand to deny the driver's claim specifically; and (2) public officers are presumed to have acted in bad faith when government-held property is released irregularly. Is the trial court's reasoning correct?

alac.answer: No. Both premises are wrong, and the mayor's conviction cannot stand on this evidence.
alac.legal_basis: The constitutional presumption of innocence protects public officers like any other accused. The burden of proving guilt beyond reasonable doubt stays with the prosecution even if the accused does not testify, and a conviction must rest on the strength of the prosecution's evidence, not on the weakness of the defense. There is no presumption of bad faith in prosecutions under R.A. No. 3019. A third person's out-of-court claim relayed by a witness without personal knowledge proves only that the claim was made. (People v. Ricketts, G.R. No. 250867, March 16, 2022, citing Suba v. Sandiganbayan and Martel v. People)
alac.application: The mayor's decision not to testify cannot fill the gap in the prosecution's evidence. Unless the prosecution first proves his participation beyond reasonable doubt, he need not present evidence at all. The court also could not presume bad faith from the irregular release, because manifest partiality or evident bad faith is an element that must be proved. The guard's testimony shows only that the driver named the mayor, not that the mayor authorized anything, so no overt act of the mayor and no conspiracy was established.
alac.conclusion: The trial court erred, and the mayor should be acquitted because his conviction rests on his silence and on a presumption of bad faith that the law does not recognize.

notes: The Court did not resolve Ricketts' procedural objection that the Sandiganbayan special division of five was not dissolved as its internal rules required; it found the issue unnecessary after acquitting him on the merits. It also did not rule on whether the warrantless OMB raid was valid. It held only that this and the other questions about the discs were not for Perez to decide.
